Where it began

Iftikhar Ali Khan Pataudi was born on 16 March 1910 at Pataudi, a small princely state not far from Delhi. He was the elder son of its Nawab, and he became Nawab himself in 1917, as a small boy. He ruled the state until 1947.

His schooling took him to Chiefs' College in Lahore, later renamed Aitchison College, where the Oxford cricketer M. G. Slater coached him. In England he had lessons from Frank Woolley, which is a fine start for any young batsman. He went up to Balliol College, Oxford, in 1927.

The player

Oxford made him wait two years for his blue. He earned it with 106 and 84 to save a match against Cambridge. In 1931 he piled up 1,307 runs for the university at an average of 93. In that summer's University Match, Cambridge's Alan Ratcliffe made a record 201. Pataudi let it be known he would top it, and the very next day he did, with 238 not out. That stood as the University Match record until 2005.

In July 1932 he made a brilliant 165 at Lord's for the Gentlemen, taking Tich Freeman's bowling apart, and that innings won him a place on that winter's tour of Australia. Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year in 1932. In the first Test of the series, at Sydney, he made 102 on debut, following Ranjitsinhji down that happy road, and England won by ten wickets. His third and last Test for England came at Trent Bridge in June 1934. Twelve years later he led India on their 1946 tour of England, and he was named Indian Cricketer of the Year for 1946/47. In six Tests in all he made 199 runs, with that one hundred as his best.

What made him special

He was a batsman of lovely footwork and plenty of appetite. In 1933, his one full season of county cricket for Worcestershire, he made 1,749 runs at 49, with two double hundreds among them. Worcestershire, never overloaded with batting, always wished they could see more of him.

If the Test figures look modest beside all that, it is partly because he gave so much of them in one go. More than half his Test runs came in that first innings at Sydney. He never seemed to do things by halves.

Away from the middle

Cricket was not his only game. He was a fine hockey player, handy at billiards and an accomplished speaker. His son, Mansoor Ali Khan Pataudi, followed him into the game and went on to captain India, so two generations of the family led India in Tests.

And finally

In 2007, to mark 75 years since India's first Test, MCC had a trophy made in his name for Test series between India and England. It seems the right prize for those two sides to play for. After all, he had been on both of them.
